sections.title: How do I know if what I'm experiencing is a genuine impulse or a behavioral adaptation?
Is it normal to feel like I'm not making progress even when I'm trying trauma release techniques?
Can I work with impulses on my own, or do I need professional help?
What if I can't identify my emotions or sensations?

blocks.p: Ever feel like you're doing all the "right" things to release trauma but keep falling back into the same stuck patterns? You're not alone, and you're definitely not doing anything wrong.

When it comes to trauma recovery, there's a significant distinction most people miss: the difference between genuine impulses that lead to healing and behavioral adaptations that keep you stuck in frustrating cycles of thought and action. Understanding this difference could be the key to finally getting the relief you're craving.
As a therapist, I regularly work with clients who feel frustrated by their lack of progress despite their best efforts.

In this piece, I'll share my thoughts on a question from a student inside the [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) ("Billy") that gets to the heart of why trauma recovery often feels like taking two steps forward and one step back.

Before we dive into the difference betwixt impulses and behavioral adaptations, let's clarify what I mean by "unstucking." You're likely reading this because you have some level of stuckness. There is an emotion or a thought or a behavior that you'd like to reduce (or banish entirely), but haven't been able to, despite your best efforts.
That's being stuck. So, unstuck is the successful reduction of whatever emotion, thought, or behavior is holding you back from the life you want to live.
What exactly are you stuck in? What is the thing that leads to the emotions, thoughts, and behaviors that you want to reduce? What's the driving force?

Stuckness isn't a way you're born. Stuck is a state of your autonomic nervous system. It's biology. When you're stuck in a defensive state, it leads to thoughts, emotions, and behaviors you want less of. Examples of a stuck autonomic nervous system are:

ul: stuck flight leads to chronic anxiety (emotion)
stuck fight leads to blaming others daily (thought)
stuck shutdown leads to isolating (behavior)

blocks.p: Why are you stuck in the first place? I don't know your life in particular, so I can't answer that, and that's far too big a question for this piece.
Unstucking isn't about achieving some perfect state where you never experience defensive responses again. That's not realistic, and it's not the goal.
When I talk about becoming "unstuck," I mean experiencing less and less stuckness over time. In other words, less and less defensive activation over time.
Unstucking does not happen all at once, no matter what "hack" or "rewiring" or whatever you're being promised. Unstucking looks like:

ul: More access to your safety state throughout the day
Increased capacity for curiosity about your internal experience
Better self-reflection abilities
Improved connection with yourself and others
Reduced intensity when defensive states do arise

blocks.p: Most of my heavily traumatized clients don't have one major breakthrough moment where suddenly they're "fixed." Instead, they experience a gradual process of steps forward, sometimes steps back, and forward again. This is completely normal and healthy.
I know you know that change is a gradual process, but do you truly accept it? Do you apply that knowing to yourself with compassion and grace?

Realistically, you know that change is gradual. Yet you still expect yourself to get magically "fixed" overnight. You would give someone else permission to make a change slowly. But you probably don't give yourself that grace.

The unstucking goal is to gradually reduce defensive activation over time through increasing access to safety and then working with defense compassionately. You're not trying to eliminate your autonomic nervous system responses. You're learning to work with them instead of against them.

blocks.h: Understanding pendulation and titration: self-regulation essentials

blocks.p: There are many skills you can use to accomplish unstucking, like students in the Unstucking Academy learn and practice on the [Unstucking Pathway](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator).
Pendulation is an advanced self-regulation skill. Titration is the process of self-regulating through small doses.
Pendulation is the natural process of moving rhythmically between defensive activation and safety. It's going from:

ul: Discomfort to comfort
Painful sensations to pleasurable ones
Defensive activation to safety anchoring

blocks.p: A natural pendulation example: When you're grieving, you might feel deep pain one moment, then remember a beautiful memory with that person the next. This back-and-forth movement is pendulation, how healthy processing happens.

One can also intentionally pendulate, focusing on a safety experience and then defensive, and back and forth. You would need to deeply anchor into your [safety state](hub:safety), then follow your inner curiosity toward stuck defense, then pendulate.

This pendulation process is an advanced skill and should only be attempted when one is sufficiently anchored into safety, and their vagal brake can tolerate the exercise. Read [the Polyvagal Theory introduction](piece:snb101-polyvagal-101-foundations) if you don't know these concepts.
Titration gradually releases a little of your defensive state at a time, not all at once. Trying to release everything altogether often leads to overwhelm, rage, or panic.

Think of it like slowly releasing pressure from a pressure cooker rather than blowing the lid off completely. One slowly releases stuck flight/fight from their system. And pendulation is one means to titrate.
Now, let's turn our attention back to impulses and behavioral adaptations.

blocks.h: The essential difference: impulses vs. behavioral adaptations

blocks.p: This is where Billy's question becomes important. They wrote:

q: "I keep thinking that acting on my impulsive shouting whenever I get caught up in a freeze state will help release this frozen energy, but I keep falling back into this state."

blocks.p: If you're acting on what feels like an "impulse" but the problem keeps resurfacing, you're likely dealing with a behavioral adaptation, not a true autonomic impulse.

Genuine autonomic impulses are behaviors that stem from an organism's Polyvagal state. They are unconscious behaviors that enable the organism to increase its chances of survival, like running or pushing a predator.

Let's frame impulses within our discussion of stuck and unstuck. When one is stuck, they have a long-held impulse that has not been acted upon. Since the impulse(s) has not been acted on, the state never changes.

Imagine a mouse shifts into its flight state because a cat is nearby. The mouse's sympathetic activation is on and is now primed to run. What happens if the mouse is unable to run because the cat has its paw on the mouse's tail?

The impulse to mobilize and create space can't be enacted. It's frozen into the system due to the immobility + flight activation. That mouse will endlessly be stuck in a lingering frozen flight activation. And its stuck state would directly influence its thoughts, emotions, and behaviors.
Therefore, impulses allow autonomic regulation. They help us transition from defense to safety. They result in less stuckness when we can enact them.
Acting on impulses enables us to shift out of stuck defense and through this autonomic sequence: immobility → mobility → connection
Examples of genuine impulses might include:

ul: From shutdown immobility: reduced stimulation, collapse, solitude
From fight/flight mobility: squeezing, pushing, pulling, sprinting, walking
From safety and connection: touch, eye contact, vocal prosody

blocks.p: So, how do you get to the underlying impulse to autonomically self-regulate? Great question! Genuine autonomic impulses emerge when you can:

ol: Identify the emotion you're experiencing (sadness, anger, anxiety)
Drill down into the sensations underneath that emotion
Mindfully experience those sensations while anchored in safety
Notice what your body actually wants to do from this grounded place

blocks.p: Behavioral adaptations feel like impulses but are actually reflexive, mindless reactions that mask underlying sensations and keep problems resurfacing:

ul: Shouting to dominate or control others
Eating, drinking, or substance use to numb feelings
Compulsive behaviors that provide temporary relief
Cutting or other self-harm behaviors

blocks.p: If you keep doing the same thing over and over but the underlying issue persists, you're likely dealing with a behavioral adaptation rather than addressing the root impulse.
Behavioral adaptations provide only a temporary reprieve, not true autonomic relief.

blocks.h: Why shouting might not be releasing your trauma

blocks.p: Let's use Billy's example of shouting during freeze states. When someone shouts, it could mean several different things:

The shouting could be an attempt to release something stuck inside. But ask yourself: Can you do this mindfully? Are you connected to the underlying sensations, or are you just reacting? And, of course, can you act on this potential impulse without taking it out on others?
The shouting might be an attempt to dominate someone else to feel powerful. This is a behavioral adaptation that temporarily masks feelings of powerlessness.
The shouting could be a desperate attempt to get someone to hear you. If this resonates, I'm more curious about the underlying experience of aloneness, fear, and immobilization that drives this need.
What emotions and sensations lie underneath the urge to shout? What is your nervous system actually trying to communicate?

blocks.h: How to access genuine impulses: a 3-step process

blocks.p: Important note: Practice this process proactively when you're regulated, not reactively when you're already dysregulated.

Another important note: I consider this a very advanced skill. Most people, especially beginners, won't have this level of connection to themselves. The [Unstucking Pathway](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) teaches Unstucking Academy students how to eventually use these steps.
Start with what you can recognize: sadness, anger, anxiety, fear. Don't try to change it, just notice it. Name it with an emotion word:

ul: "I feel sad."
"I feel confused."
"I feel frustrated."

blocks.prompt: Name what you feel right now with one emotion word: "I feel ____."

blocks.p: Ask yourself: "What does this emotion feel like in my body?" This step is very difficult for most people. If you struggle with it, congrats, you're normal.
For sadness, sensations might be:

ul: heaviness
a bowling ball in the belly, or void, or cold
Numbness throughout your body

blocks.p: From a place of safety and curiosity, ask: "What does my body need right now? What wants to happen?" The safety piece of this is the most important. You need to be anchored in your safety state.

This is where genuine impulses emerge, but only if you're anchored in enough safety to listen without judgment. When you're anchored and connected to your body's needs, only then may an impulse emerge.

blocks.h: The safety foundation: why this process requires regulation

blocks.p: This is essential and always overlooked: You must be grounded in safety to access genuine impulses. Without this foundation, you'll keep cycling through behavioral adaptations.
Building this safety foundation involves:

ul: Identifying what brings you to safety (your personal anchors)
Developing your "vagal brake" (your capacity to handle distress)
Balancing safety and defense (mindfully and proactively)
Learning to observe your internal experience with curiosity rather than judgment

blocks.p: There's a paradox here: To heal your defensive states, you first need enough safety to feel them fully. This is why trauma recovery requires building your safety capacity before diving into the deeper work.

I hear far too often from clients that they have been through modalities like EMDR or Trauma-Focused CBT and ended up re-traumatizing themselves because they lacked the safety capacity to benefit. We only touch upon defense when ready.

blocks.why: You need to be anchored in safety before an impulse can come. This practice is that anchoring, tuned to you.

blocks.p: If you're stuck in freeze like Billy, remember that freeze involves both mobilization (fight/flight) AND immobilization (shutdown) happening simultaneously.
[Freeze and shutdown are not the same.](piece:freeze-vs-shutdown) Freeze is a tense, rigid experience rather than the collapsed one of shutdown.
When working with freeze:

ol: Prioritize anchoring into safety. This will thaw the immobility and open the chance to utilize the once-frozen flight/fight activation.

As the once-frozen flight/fight emerges, mindfully welcome it and choose to use it through something you enjoy, like movement or creativity. It's possible to mindfully feel the emerging flight/fight and allow a spontaneous expression of it in the body, but this is more advanced and requires a very strong safety state.
Work with a polyvagal-informed therapist if [freeze states](hub:freeze) persist

blocks.p: For more support with shutdown states specifically, read my comprehensive guide on [understanding dorsal vagal shutdown](piece:dorsal-vagal-shutdown). And for a deeper understanding of how freeze differs from other states, read my complete [Polyvagal Theory introduction](piece:snb101-polyvagal-101-foundations).

blocks.h: When behavioral adaptations serve a purpose

blocks.p: Before we demonize behavioral adaptations, let's acknowledge something important: they often represent your best attempt at self-regulation given your current capacity.

Substance use, emotional eating, or even compulsive behaviors might be attempts to manage overwhelming nervous system activation. The goal isn't to judge these responses but to gradually build capacity for more effective regulation. As you build regulation, the behavioral adaptations may decrease over time, especially if you're making small behavioral changes, too.
No, behavioral adaptations are not ideal. Far from it. And yes, we want them to stop. However, adding judgment on top of them doesn't help either.
As best you can, give yourself compassion and understanding. (And if you can't, try not to judge yourself for it!)
You'll know you're working with true impulses rather than behavioral adaptations when:

ul: The behavior feels curious rather than compulsive
You can stay present and aware during the experience
There's a sense of completion or release afterward
The underlying issue gradually improves over time
You feel more regulated, not more dysregulated

blocks.h: Practical steps for your trauma recovery journey

blocks.p: What are some next-step options?
This is paramount. I continually tell clients and students that the priority in unstucking is always ensuring safety. Before pendulating, we begin in safety, maintain safety, and end in safety.
Before diving into trauma release work, ensure you can:

ul: Identify what brings you to your safety state
Access curiosity about your internal experience
Stay present with mild discomfort without becoming overwhelmed

blocks.p: We're never done building safety, by the way. It's always relevant. And our safety state always needs strengthening to not only deal with daily life, but also welcome new challenges.

Personally, I practice mindfulness daily in small doses, like looking out a window in the morning, taking an intentional breath in the afternoon, and connecting with family in meaningful ways in the evening.
As your system allows, regularly practice moving from emotion → sensation → impulse when you're NOT in crisis. This builds your capacity for when you need it most.
If this is too difficult, don't worry about it for now. Return to it later after you've built more capacity. In the meantime, focus on building your safety state through intentional and repeated:

ul: practicing mindfulness daily, even in micro-moments
anchoring into safety and then permitting defensive activation as well
pendulating between safety and defense

blocks.p: If you find yourself resistant to healing, this isn't a character flaw. Often, resistance indicates your nervous system has unmet needs. Learn more about working with this in my article on [polyvagal resistance](piece:polyvagal-resistance).
Consider working with a polyvagal-informed therapist if:

ul: You're stuck in an unmanageable defensive state
Your attempts at self-regulation aren't creating lasting change
You need support building your safety foundation

blocks.p: Remember Billy's original question about why they kept "falling back" into freeze states? This isn't about willpower or doing something wrong. Trauma recovery is a biological process that requires patience, curiosity, and often professional guidance.
True impulses emerge from a place of safety and lead to regulation. Behavioral adaptations emerge from dysregulation and keep you stuck in dysfunctional cycles.

Your nervous system isn't broken. It's trying to communicate important information. Learning to listen to these communications rather than imposing predetermined outcomes is the path to genuine recovery.

blocks.h3: How do I know if what I'm experiencing is a genuine impulse or a behavioral adaptation?

blocks.p: Genuine impulses emerge from a place of safety and curiosity, lead to a sense of completion, and gradually resolve the underlying issue. Behavioral adaptations feel compulsive, provide only temporary relief, and keep the same problems surfacing repeatedly.

blocks.h3: Is it normal to feel like I'm not making progress even when I'm trying trauma release techniques?

blocks.p: Absolutely. Most people experience a gradual process rather than dramatic breakthroughs. If techniques aren't working, you may need to build more safety capacity first, or you might be working with behavioral adaptations rather than addressing underlying impulses.

blocks.h3: Can I work with impulses on my own, or do I need professional help?

blocks.p: While self-awareness is valuable, working with genuine trauma impulses often benefits from professional guidance, especially if you're dealing with complex trauma or freeze states. A polyvagal-informed therapist can help you build safety capacity and navigate the process safely.

blocks.h3: What if I can't identify my emotions or sensations?

blocks.p: This is common, especially if you've been in defensive states for a long time. Start by building your safety state capacity first. As your nervous system feels safer, your ability to sense internal experiences will naturally improve.

"You're not broken; you're stuck. And biology, not willpower, is the key to getting unstuck."
